title: Why September 3 Is a Pivotal Date for International Students on F-1 and J-1 Visas
excerpt: A federal court hearing on September 3 could determine whether the DHS rule ending decades-old "duration of status" protections for F and J visa holders takes effect on September 15 — or gets blocked by an injunction.
body:
• A federal court hearing on September 3, 2026 will consider a preliminary injunction that could block the DHS rule ending "duration of status" for F-1 and J-1 visa holders before it takes effect on September 15.
  • A coalition of universities, unions, and advocacy groups sued DHS on August 18, arguing the rule could disrupt degree completion, physician training, and trigger economic harm if international enrollment falls.
  • The new rule caps F and J visa stays at four years, requires USCIS extension applications with biometric screening and background checks, and cuts the F-1 post-completion grace period from 60 to 30 days.
  • Major universities including Harvard, Columbia, Ohio State, and Georgetown are urging international students to return to the US before September 15 to avoid being readmitted under the new fixed-term system.

The September 3 Court Hearing

For the roughly 1.5 million international students and exchange visitors currently in the United States on F and J visas, September 3 has emerged as a critical date. A federal court is scheduled to hear arguments that day on a preliminary injunction that could block — or allow — a sweeping new Department of Homeland Security rule from taking effect on September 15.

A coalition of universities, labor unions, and immigrant advocacy groups filed suit against DHS on August 18, seeking to halt the regulation. The court set a government response deadline of August 31 and scheduled an in-person hearing on the injunction for September 3. The outcome could determine whether millions of visa holders face an entirely new immigration framework when the fall semester begins.

What the New Rule Changes

The DHS rule, finalized on July 17 after receiving nearly 22,000 public comments, eliminates the decades-old "duration of status" system that allowed F-1 students and J-1 exchange visitors to remain in the United States for as long as they maintained valid enrollment in their academic programs.

Under the new framework, international students will receive fixed periods of admission capped at four years. Those who need more time to complete their degrees — a common situation for doctoral candidates in STEM fields, whose programs routinely run five to seven years — must file formal extension applications with US Citizenship and Immigration Services.

Those extensions will require biometric vetting, background checks, and fraud screening, according to DHS. The rule also shortens the F-1 post-completion grace period from 60 days to 30 days, giving graduates less time to arrange their departure or transition to work authorization.

"International students and exchange visitors are already the most tracked of all nonimmigrant categories in the United States."

— NAFSA: Association of International Educators

Universities Sound the Alarm

Major US universities are not waiting for the court to decide. Harvard, Columbia, Ohio State, Georgetown, the University of Chicago, and dozens of other institutions have issued advisories urging international students currently abroad to return to the United States before September 15.

Columbia University recommended that all students return to New York City before classes begin on September 8. The university said it would host a webinar with immigration attorney Dan Berger and provide direct email updates to students under its F-1 and J-1 sponsorship.

Auburn University published detailed guidance explaining that students entering or re-entering the US on or after September 15 will receive a specific "Admit Until Date" on their Form I-94, rather than the open-ended D/S notation that has been standard for decades. The University of Kansas and Northeastern University have issued similar advisories.

The Stakes for Indian Students

Indian students, who form the second-largest international student population in the US after Chinese nationals, face disproportionate impact from the new rule. According to analysis by LawStreet, the four-year cap creates an immediate structural problem for Indian PhD scholars, whose programs in science, engineering, and medicine routinely exceed four years.

The rule also adds uncertainty to Optional Practical Training — the post-study work authorization that allows STEM graduates to work in the US for up to three years. OPT has been one of the central reasons Indian students choose American universities over institutions in the UK, Canada, or Australia. A mandatory USCIS review at the extension stage introduces a new bureaucratic hurdle into a pathway that has been the primary on-ramp to H-1B sponsorship and eventual permanent residency.

About 1.5 million current F and J visa holders will automatically transition to the new system when it takes effect. In 2023 alone, more than 1.6 million F-1 students and over 500,000 J exchange visitors were admitted to the United States.

What Happens Next

If the court grants the preliminary injunction on September 3, the rule's implementation could be paused while the legal challenge proceeds. If it denies the injunction, the new framework takes effect on September 15 as planned.

Universities warn that practical details remain unclear, and the rule could trigger a surge of USCIS filings, processing delays, higher costs for students, and increased risk of inadvertent unlawful presence for those in multi-year programs. Plaintiffs in the lawsuit have cited studies projecting significant economic harm if international enrollment declines as a result.

For Indian students and their families, the September 3 hearing is the last checkpoint before a fundamental shift in how the United States manages its international student population.
